title: Kernel-selection + quantization rollout decision log
summary: Architectural review for RFC: adaptive kernel selection paired with 4-bit quantized execution. Goal: pick an implementation approach that meets p95 latency SLOs across mix of seq-len workloads while enabling safe rollback when quality or perf regressions are detected.
background: We have two parallel efforts: (1) compiler/runtime work to support multiple kernel implementations for the same op (float16 vs quantized int4/int8) and (2) model onboarding where some models show large perf wins under quantization but risk small quality regressions. Prior experiments showed 30-60% throughput improvement on A100-40GB for int4 kernels, but with variable p99 tail behavior for long seq workloads and occasional token-level divergence. This meeting evaluates proposals for selection logic, caching, and rollout/rollback policy. Related context: KV prefix caching RFC (see linked_artifacts) and previous multi-variant routing notes.
proposals: Proposal A - Static mapping at model-version: Maintain a per-model-version profile (compiled offline). For a given model+version+target-sequence-distribution we cache the best kernel set in the model catalog. Runtime simply looks up kernel set when routing to a backend. Pros: simple, predictable. Cons: brittle for workload shifts and doesn't adapt to per-request latency spikes.

Proposal B - Dynamic per-request selector: Add a lightweight runtime decision path that picks kernels per request based on request metadata (max_tokens, temperature, user tier) and recent SLO signals from local monitoring. Pros: responsive to workload changes and can degrade to safe kernels quickly. Cons: more complex, potential CPU overhead on hot paths, needs fast-path microbenchmarks.

Proposal C - Hybrid per-batch selection with fallback: Select kernels per micro-batch using heuristics (batch token count, sequence length histogram sampled from the batch) with an automatic fallback policy to FP16 kernels when local p95 exceeds threshold. Also includes a compile-time prioritized kernel list (quantized-first, fp16-fallback). Pros: balances stability+adaptiveness and limits selector frequency. Cons: requires batching-aware hooks and accurate batch metadata.

Proposal D - Canary-first rollout: Keep runtime simple (static/catalog lookup) but rely on Canary pipeline tied to real traffic experiments. Canary verifies token-level evals and SLO telemetry before promoting to catalog default. This moves complexity to infra and CI harness rather than runtime. Pros: minimal runtime complexity. Cons: slower to react and requires richer canary infra and tagging.
decision: Adopt Proposal C (Hybrid per-batch selection) as the default implementation path, paired with a Canary-first promotion for model catalog entries. Rationale: hybrid approach gives strong perf wins while containing tail risk via batch-level heuristics and automatic fallback. Canary promotion reduces risk of silent quality regressions by gating catalog updates with token-level evals and SLO checks.
tradeoffs:
- Complexity: Slight increase to batching path and additional telemetry points. Implementation must be low-overhead to avoid adding CPU cost to the critical token generation loop.
- Safety: Hybrid reduces risk but doesn't eliminate subtle token-level regressions; hence Canary promotion and QA evals are mandatory.
- Observability burden: need new per-batch metrics (selected_kernel, fallback_count, batch_seq_hist) and correlation with token-level regressions for alerts.
- Storage/compile cost: we will store multiple compiled kernel variants per model version, increasing artifact storage and build runtime.
benchmarks: Planned benchmark harness: local/scale tests across 3 representative model shapes: small-chat (3B), base-llm (13B), and long-context (70B). Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, memory per replica, percent fallback-to-fp16, token-level divergence (BLEU+perplexity proxy) on canonical eval prompt set. Baseline: current FP16 catalog. Targets: >=30% tokens/sec improvement for int4 on 13B with p95 within 1.2x of baseline and p99 not exceeding 1.5x baseline; divergence < 0.5% token edit rate on eval set for canary promotion. Bench infra: use dedicated perf fleet plumbing (perf-cluster-3) and reproduceable load generator (perfgen v2).

rollout_plan: 1) Implement hybrid selector behind feature flag (off by default). 2) Run internal perf jobs with feature flag enabled on nightly perf cluster; collect telemetry for 1 week. 3) Enable canary promotion pipeline for a small percent of real traffic (1-2%). 4) If token-level evals & SLO pass for canary cohort, promote kernel set in model catalog for targeted models; gradually increase traffic. 5) Keep automatic fallback thresholds conservative for first 2 weeks post-promote. Rollback criteria: sustained p95 > 1.4x baseline for >30 minutes OR token-edit-rate > threshold on canary traffic.
open_questions: How to choose batch-level histogram sampling frequency to minimize overhead but maintain selector accuracy?
Should selected_kernel be returned to caller in traces or anonymized? (privacy vs debug)
What is acceptable storage retention for compiled artifacts when model versions churn quickly?
Do we need an additional ML-driven selector in future or will heuristics suffice? Timeline?
notes: Meeting contained several short debates: Priya pushed for stricter rollback to avoid customer-visible regressions; Marcus argued selector overhead looked negligible in microbenchmarks but needs validation under high qps. Rina recommended building dashboard first to surfacing regressions quickly. Jonah emphasized token-level evals must be part of canary pipeline otherwise regression blindspots exist. Action owners agreed on dates. Follow-up: 30-min sync next Monday to review Marcus PoC and initial perf runs. Refer to linked PR for initial code sketch and Linear issue for tracking.
